name: Aaron Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Aaron. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We aren't tied to tech companies, employers, unions or parties, and what you say stays confidential. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee negotiator at Ashdown Property, an independent agency on the edge of a fast-growing town. A lot of our work is selling new-build houses for a local developer on the Meadowfield estate, plus normal resales. Mornings I'm in the show home, afternoons I'm doing viewings and ringing buyers about their mortgages. I like the show home, people walk in excited and you get to be part of that.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Remembering all the details, like which plot has the bigger garden and which has the south-facing one. Mark Ashdown, the owner, knows every plot by heart and I still check my sheet. I use an AI chat thing now and then to write up the plot details, but I don't trust it with numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool like any other and the market will decide what it's worth. At work I'd say it's handy for the boring bits. I'd probably share a joke about it online, nothing serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, that's fine for me. I'd keep learning the trade from Mark, and I've got my grandad's old flat that I rent out, so I've got income on the side. Grace, my girlfriend, works as a teaching assistant, and we're comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Ashdown and aim to be a full negotiator within two years. I'd keep using the AI for plot write-ups when I'm busy. I'd keep the rent from the flat going into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the flat. How did that come about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandad left me his one-bed above the bakery on Church Street when he died three years ago. I fixed it up with my dad, who's a scaffolder, over a few weekends. The rent covers its own costs and leaves me about three hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything in this world that would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interest rates, mostly. If interest rates go up, people stop buying new-builds and the show home goes quiet. Rates move our numbers, not computers.

I'd joke online and call it handy for **boring bits**.
think: I'd keep **learning the trade** from the owner, Mark.
My grandad's **rented flat** gives me income on the side.
do: **Aim for full negotiator** within two years.
Keep using AI for **plot write-ups** when busy.

His **free-market** framing comes through even in small talk.

steps.text: Work towards full negotiator at Ashdown Property within two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say jobs change and people adapt, they always have. At work I'd say let's learn what's useful and ignore the rest. I wouldn't want the government stepping in with lots of rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the show home is safe for a while because people want to walk round a house. But the mortgage chasing, the plot details, the follow-up emails, that's the card exactly. Mark might not need a trainee like me to do the paperwork side anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd learn the new tools once Leon, the senior negotiator, had tried them and they worked. I'd push to spend more time in the show home and on viewings, the face-to-face part. And I'd keep saving the rent from the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. Not worried exactly, just keeping an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't want the government stepping in. What if lots of people lost jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd want them helped into proper training. My dad's a scaffolder and he learned on the job. If people lose jobs, help them into apprenticeships, not just hand them money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Grace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Grace not to worry, because we've got the flat and savings. I'd also say I might need to work some weekends in the show home to stay useful. She'd roll her eyes, she hates me working Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a shock, but people will find a way, they always do. I'd say government should get out of the way of businesses creating new jobs. At work I'd keep my head down and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the trainee job goes. If AI can do the thinking work by 2028, it can sell a new-build from a screen, and the developer would cut the agency out. The show home could need a person until robots arrive around 2031, but that's not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the flat and its rent as my steady income, and cut back on spending, like the new car I was saving for. I'd look at hands-on work for the next few years, maybe joining my dad's scaffolding firm. Grace's job is in a school, so it might last longer than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not panicking. I've got the flat and family, which a lot of people don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scaffolding is very different from selling houses. Would you really do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, yes. I've done summers with my dad since I was sixteen, and I'm not scared of heights. Scaffolding is honest work and it pays decently. Robots won't be climbing scaffolds for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said government should get out of the way. If your own job went, would you want any help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe help with training costs, for a scaffolding card or a trade course. But I'd rather lean on my family first. That's what families are for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to get ready, so let's not panic. At work I'd say we should be learning the tools and building our local name. I'd say businesses will adapt faster than politicians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably be okay. Five years gives me time to save more, maybe buy a second small flat to rent. I'd still expect the trainee job to shrink, but I'd have options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools more at Ashdown, since they'd become normal. I'd save hard for a deposit on a second rental flat within three years. If the agency job started fading, I'd move to my dad's firm around 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control. It's a plan, not a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't a second flat risky if lots of people lose their jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yes, that's fair. People always need somewhere to live. I'd rather own bricks than have money sitting in a bank. I'd pick something cheap near the station.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Grace about the next five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Grace we stick to the plan: save, buy the second flat, then think about marriage and kids around 2029. She'd want the wedding sooner. We'd probably meet in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the market will sort out who's needed. At work I'd keep doing the job well. I'd say the same to my mates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the comfortable one. Ten years gives me time to become a full negotiator, buy a second flat, and maybe a third. By 2036 I'd be a small landlord with a trade to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Ashdown and push to become a senior negotiator. I'd buy a second flat in a few years and fix it up with my dad. I'd use AI tools when everyone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with a small worry in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the small worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone has the same idea as me and buys flats, and then there are fewer tenants with jobs to pay the rent. If lots of people lose work after 2036, rents could drop. I'd want to keep the debt on my flats low to be safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still think about the scaffolding firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe later. My dad wants to retire around 2035, and someone has to take it on. It might make sense for me to learn it properly over the decade.

I'd keep **doing the job well** and say so to mates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd lose the job before I'd had time to build anything. What would help is cheap trade training and less red tape for small firms like my dad's, so they can take more people on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about who owns houses. If AI makes lots of people poorer, the people with property will be fine and the rest won't. I know I'm one of the lucky ones. That's thanks to my grandad, and I think about it.

He owns his grandad's **rented flat**, which gives him side income in every scenario.
He uses AI **now and then** and waits for colleagues to prove tools first.
His **traditional views** show in trust in markets, family and apprenticeships over handouts.
In fast scenarios he'd **join his dad's scaffolding** firm; with time he'd build up rental flats.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the job goes before he can build anything.
